paper: Gopal & Trefethen, New Laplace and Helmholtz solvers, PNAS 116(21):10223-10225 (2019); companion arXiv:1905.02960 (SINUM 57(5):2074-2094, 2019)
verdict_context: REPLICATED on the L-shape showcase; these questions are the genuinely OPEN follow-ups that the replication did NOT settle.

questions.q: Does the Helmholtz variant of the lightning solver — analytic-kernel rational-plus-polynomial ansatz with exponentially clustered exterior poles — retain root-exponential convergence uniformly in the wavenumber k, or does the required pole density and clustering parameter σ scale unfavorably with k (e.g. as k grows the far-field oscillations force N ~ k or worse)?
questions.basis: The paper is titled 'New Laplace AND Helmholtz solvers' and the PNAS note explicitly promises a Helmholtz extension using the same fixed-pole LSQ machinery, but our replication only exercised the Laplace case. C4 (performance vs FEM) and the Helmholtz claim are both untested in this replication. Root-exponential convergence in N is well-established for |x|-type corner singularities of harmonic functions (Newman 1964); the analogous statement for Helmholtz has to contend with an intrinsic oscillation length ~1/k that could add a k-dependent constant or destroy root-exponential entirely at high k.
next_steps: Reimplement the ansatz with a Helmholtz fundamental solution (Hankel H_0^{(1)}(k|z-z_j|)) in place of 1/(z-z_j), keeping the same clustered-pole geometry.
Run a k-sweep (k = 1, 4, 16, 64) on the same L-shape with a manufactured Helmholtz solution (e.g. an incident plane wave scattered by a Dirichlet edge) and fit err vs sqrt(N) at each k.

Diagnose whether the fitted exponent C(k) is roughly k-independent, decays like 1/k, or degrades to algebraic — that separates 'method extends cleanly' from 'method extends but with k-dependent cost' from 'method fails at high k'.

questions.q: For polygons with MULTIPLE reentrant corners (e.g. slit domains, cross-shaped domains, or the classic dumbbell), does per-corner tapered pole density remain sufficient, or does the linear least-squares system become ill-conditioned in a way not captured by the single-reentrant L-shape — specifically, do the clustered pole clouds from neighboring reentrant corners begin to 'see' each other and produce near-linear-dependence in the LSQ columns?
questions.basis: Our best config used HEAVY clustering (n_re=44) at the ONE reentrant corner of the L-shape and LIGHT clustering (n_c=3) at each of the five convex corners. That worked because reentrant corners were geometrically isolated. The paper informally recommends per-corner tapering but does not systematically explore multi-reentrant geometries. Our own convergence table shows boundary maxerr rising at n_re >= 36 — the well-known conditioning floor. With K reentrant corners, each contributing O(n_re) tightly-spaced exterior poles, the effective condition number of the ~3N x N Vandermonde-like matrix could scale super-linearly in K.
next_steps: Add second_geom_multireentrant.py that constructs a cross domain (four reentrant 270° corners) and a slit domain (one 360° reentrant), and repeats the C1-style challenge with a manufactured harmonic datum.
Track cond(A) of the real LSQ matrix as a function of (K_reentrant, n_re) and see whether the conditioning penalty for adding reentrant corners is additive, multiplicative, or worse.
If ill-conditioned, try Arnoldi orthogonalization on the POLE block too (not just the polynomial block) — this is a documented Brubeck–Nakatsukasa–Trefethen 2021 improvement we did NOT apply here.

questions.q: How sensitive are the paper's 8-digit accuracy claims to the exact clustering law d_k = exp(−σ (√n − √k))? In particular, is the sqrt-spacing FORM (Newman/Stahl-style) genuinely necessary, or would competing analytically-motivated spacings — Zolotarev-optimal points, tanh-sinh, or a learned/optimized spacing — give strictly better error at the same DOF budget?
questions.basis: The paper's clustering law is motivated by Newman's 1964 root-exponential result for rational approximation of |x|, which is asymptotic and gives the CORRECT rate but not necessarily the OPTIMAL prefactor. Our fine-grid sweep varied σ and n but held the sqrt spacing FORM fixed. Zolotarev's optimal rational approximants are known to give the sharp exponential constant for related problems (sign function, matrix square root); porting them here would tighten the C constant in exp(−C sqrt(N)). Practically important because our best C=1.95 (interior) leaves headroom before the machine-precision floor.
next_steps: Implement two alternative spacings in lightning_v3.py: (a) Zolotarev points scaled to the outward corner bisector, (b) tanh-sinh spacing.
For each spacing, sweep σ (or its analog) at fixed n_re=32,40 on the L-shape challenge and record fitted C.

Also try an OPTIMIZED spacing: nonlinear LSQ over pole positions (few extra unknowns) as a control — if optimized poles beat sqrt-clustering by <5% in C, sqrt-clustering is essentially optimal; if by >20%, there's a genuinely new spacing to publish.

questions.q: Does the lightning ansatz extend to the BIHARMONIC equation (Δ²u = 0, needed for Stokes flow and Kirchhoff plate bending) with the same clustered-pole + LSQ machinery, and if so what is the correct analog of the rational basis — Goursat representation via TWO holomorphic functions each with their own clustered-pole expansion, or a single hyper-analytic expansion?
questions.basis: Trefethen and collaborators have follow-up work (Brubeck–Trefethen 2022, LP+AAA-style extensions) suggesting the lightning idea DOES port to biharmonic/Stokes via the Goursat representation u = Re(z̄·φ(z) + χ(z)) with clustered-pole rationals for φ and χ. This replication only covered harmonic (Laplace). Testing biharmonic would be a substantive extension because (a) Stokes flow in polygonal cavities has direct engineering relevance, (b) the Goursat splitting doubles the DOF count and it is not obvious the LSQ conditioning survives, (c) reentrant-corner singularity exponents for biharmonic (Dean–Montagnon 1949, ~0.544) differ from harmonic (~2/3 for the L-shape).
next_steps: Implement biharmonic_lightning.py using Goursat: two Arnoldi-orthogonalized rational-plus-polynomial expansions φ(z), χ(z) with clustered poles at each corner.
Validate on driven-cavity Stokes flow on a rectangle (known series solution) at machine precision, then on the L-shape driven cavity (moving lid) where corner eddies of Moffatt type appear.

Fit err vs sqrt(N) and compare the exponential rate constant to the Laplace value — if C_biharmonic ≈ 0.5 · C_Laplace (matching the ratio of singularity exponents), that's strong evidence the method generalizes structurally.

questions.q: What is the QUANTITATIVE performance/accuracy break-even against high-order p-FEM or hp-FEM on the same L-shape challenge — specifically, at what target accuracy tolerance does lightning become faster than a well-tuned hp-FEM with geometric mesh refinement at the reentrant corner, and does the crossover point move with problem size (single point evaluation vs full-domain error norm)?
questions.basis: The paper claims 'beats FEM for high-accuracy corner problems' and 'sub-second laptop solves' but presents no timing table against a state-of-the-art FEM package. Our C4 was explicitly marked 'not benchmarked'. This is the single most important open question for the method's practical uptake: hp-FEM with geometric mesh refinement at reentrant corners (Schwab 1998) is KNOWN to achieve exponential convergence in DOF for corner problems, so the fair comparison is lightning vs hp-FEM, not lightning vs uniform-order FEM. Without this benchmark the paper's headline productivity claim is untested.
next_steps: Run the L-shape challenge in NGSolve or MFEM using hp-FEM with geometric refinement toward (1,1), matching target tolerances tol = 1e-4, 1e-6, 1e-8, 1e-10.
For each tol, record wall-clock time and DOFs for hp-FEM and for the lightning solver, on the SAME laptop, single-threaded.

Report a Pareto frontier (time vs achieved accuracy) — expected shape: hp-FEM wins at loose tol due to lower setup overhead, lightning wins at tight tol due to root-exponential vs exponential-in-DOF but with a favorable constant. Publish the crossover tolerance; that's the number the paper should have shown.
